title: Set DefaultTimeoutStopSec=5s for systemd user session manager

workflow: Opus full review, Sol boundary hunter, Opus self-check of the draft, editorial check, batch gates

leads.summary: P2: Equal 5s inner and outer deadlines do not reserve time for orderly user-manager shutdown
leads.consequence: When a user scope/service consumes its full default 5s stopping period, PID 1 can reach the explicit 5s user@.service deadline at the same time. This cannot guarantee that the user manager delivers its own SIGKILL, handles remaining units and exits before PID 1 kills the manager. The file really changes the user-manager unit default, but it does not establish the described orderly-shutdown ordering. Allow headroom in the outer timeout or avoid claiming a guaranteed ordering. Source-verified, not live-reproduced.
leads.triage: corroborates; Same as Opus Finding 2 (published as finding 2).

leads.summary: P2: New global drop-in overrides a user's existing user.conf timeout
leads.consequence: A user who set DefaultTimeoutStopSec=30s in ~/.config/systemd/user.conf previously had that 30s manager default, but after this drop-in is loaded the 5s value wins because all user.conf.d files are parsed after the main user.conf, even the main file in the user's home directory. Services and app scopes without explicit per-unit timeouts now receive 5s despite this explicit user configuration. The user must migrate the preference to a later-sorted user.conf.d drop-in, or the distro should document/avoid overriding that main-file setting. Source-verified, not live-reproduced.
leads.triage: verified_factual; Coordinator read systemd v262 man/standard-conf.xml: conf.d drop-ins override main files. Opus self-check refined: only DefaultTimeoutStopSec from ~/.config/systemd/user.conf is overridden; user drop-in must sort after 10-faster-shutdown.conf. Published as optional note.

leads.summary: P2: Per-user migration unconditionally rewrites one global /etc config file
leads.consequence: The command `tee /etc/systemd/user.conf.d/10-faster-shutdown.conf` truncates any existing file without checking its contents or whether it was customized. Completion markers are per user, so even after one user's migration finishes, running migrations for a second account later repeats the write and can erase an administrator's 10-faster-shutdown.conf edits. If a writable target is a symlink, tee follows it. Guard existing content or gate the global write once, and leave a distinct admin override intact. Source-verified, not executed against /etc.
leads.triage: merged; Overwriting admin edits is subsumed by Opus Finding 1, whose suggested change removes the migration.

leads.summary: P2: Add new file to stable omarchy-settings backup=() list
leads.consequence: package() copies `etc/.` to `/etc`, so this new file becomes package-owned when built with this PR, but the stable recipe's pacman backup list names both existing faster-shutdown siblings and not `etc/systemd/user.conf.d/10-faster-shutdown.conf`. On a subsequent settings upgrade, pacman can replace administrator edits to the new file rather than saving the new content as .pacnew. Add that exact relative path after the existing system/user@ faster-shutdown entries. Source-verified, no package transaction run.
leads.triage: corroborates; Opus optional note (backup=() companion); published as optional note.

leads.summary: P2: Add same new file to omarchy-settings-dev backup=() list
leads.consequence: The dev settings recipe also ships the whole etc tree and its backup list contains the two existing faster-shutdown siblings but not this new user-manager file. A dev-channel machine changing that file can lose its edits on the next settings-dev upgrade. Add `etc/systemd/user.conf.d/10-faster-shutdown.conf` alongside the existing faster-shutdown paths here too. Source-verified, no package transaction run.

leads.summary: P2: #9070 deletes the overwrite list this PR edits, making their upgrade changes incompatible without reconciliation
leads.consequence: Open, unstacked #9070 moves all file takeovers into one early omarchy-settings install with `--overwrite='*'` and replaces the entire final pacman `--overwrite` list with a plain `pacman -Syu`. This PR appends a flag to precisely that list; a valid three-way merge produces a conflict. Resolving in favor of #9070 without changing this PR's test leaves test/shell.d/systemd-test.sh:114 failing because the flag is absent, while keeping the list breaks #9070's explicit one-time ownership boundary. Rebase and adapt the test to assert the actual package adoption path if #9070 lands. Source-verified, merge simulated as text only.
leads.triage: verified_factual; Coordinator verified with gh api: #9070 open (dirty), removes the final --overwrite list. Opus self-check git merge-file: exactly 1 conflict with this PR's line, 0 without. Published in Details; Opus final had missed it.

leads.summary: P3: New static assertions pass without either a migration or a valid Manager section
leads.consequence: Two plausible broken implementations leave the new success line green: remove migrations/1789235400.sh (existing users do not receive the repair on the migration-only path), or put DefaultTimeoutStopSec=5s under [Service] instead of [Manager] (systemd ignores it in user.conf.d). Both mutants pass the unchanged test with exit 0 because it checks the file and raw line, not its parsed section or the migration. Add a check of the section and a migration content/behaviour test, not another substring grep. Reproduced in sealed review.py sandbox runs, see reproducers/missing-migration-test.md.
leads.triage: corroborates; Opus [Service] mutant; published as optional note. Untested migration point moot after suggested removal.

## Automated AI review

> **Community review:** Independent automated community review, unaffiliated with the Omarchy team, intended to help prepare PRs for their review.

**Outcome:** The migration needs sudo for a file the package already installs, blocking later migrations for users without sudo.

### Migration is redundant and fails without sudo

`omarchy-settings` already installs the drop-in in the same upgrade, yet the migration runs `sudo mkdir` and `sudo tee` for every user. **Impact:** without sudo it exits 1, leaving it and all later migrations pending.

**Suggested change:** remove the migration, plus the new `--overwrite` line and its test assertion.

<details><summary>Reproducer (fails at 8fe19d0)</summary>

### Reproducer: migration 1789235400 needs sudo for a file the package already installs

Tested at PR head `8fe19d0d5be79b2468ef392977a7337cfada94a5`. `sudo` is a stub that refuses, as it does for an account outside sudoers; nothing runs with privilege.

**1. Test in the repository's shell-test style.** Save as `test/shell.d/user-shutdown-timeout-migration-test.sh` and run `bash test/shell.d/user-shutdown-timeout-migration-test.sh` from the repository root.

```bash
#!/bin/bash

set -euo pipefail

source "$(cd -- "$(dirname -- "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)/base-test.sh"

migration="$ROOT/migrations/1789235400.sh"
test_dir=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$test_dir"' EXIT

mkdir -p "$test_dir/bin" "$test_dir/home"
cat >"$test_dir/bin/sudo" <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
printf 'sudo %s\n' "$*" >>"$SUDO_LOG"
echo "user is not in the sudoers file." >&2
exit 1
EOF
chmod +x "$test_dir/bin/sudo"

# omarchy-settings copies etc/ into /etc, and omarchy pins omarchy-settings to
# its own version, so the drop-in is already installed when this migration
# runs. Migrations run once per user; a user who cannot sudo must still get
# through this one, or every later migration stays pending for them.
if ! HOME="$test_dir/home" SUDO_LOG="$test_dir/sudo.log" PATH="$test_dir/bin:$PATH" OMARCHY_PATH="$ROOT" \
  bash -euo pipefail "$migration" >/dev/null 2>"$test_dir/stderr"; then
  fail "migration completes for a user without sudo" "$(cat "$test_dir/sudo.log" "$test_dir/stderr")"
fi
[[ ! -s $test_dir/sudo.log ]] ||
  fail "migration does not ask for root to rewrite a file omarchy-settings already installs" "$(cat "$test_dir/sudo.log")"
pass "migration leaves the packaged drop-in to omarchy-settings"
```

Output at the PR head (exit status 1):

```

user is not in the sudoers file.
not ok - migration completes for a user without sudo
```

With the migration's `as_root mkdir` and `as_root tee` lines deleted, the same test prints (exit status 0):

ok - migration leaves the packaged drop-in to omarchy-settings

### Equal 5 s timeouts do not change shutdown

PID 1's 5 s `user@.service` timer starts before any user unit's 5 s timer, so a hung unit still ends with PID 1 killing the manager. **Impact:** shutdown is unchanged; logout and in-session stops are capped at 5 s, not 90 s. Source analysis, not reproduced.

**Suggested change:** describe it as bounding logout, or set the user default below 5 s if the user manager should finish first.

<details><summary>Details</summary>

**Shutdown order (systemd v262 source):**

```text
PID 1: stop user@.service -> SIGTERM to systemd --user, arm 5 s timer   (service.c service_enter_signal)
user manager: receives SIGTERM -> starts exit.target -> each unit's 5 s timer starts when its stop job runs
PID 1 timer fires first (or in the same 250 ms coalescing window) -> SIGKILL to the whole user@ cgroup (KillMode=mixed)
```

Upstream `user@.service` uses `TimeoutStopSec` = 4/3 of the user default (120 s against 90 s) for this margin. The cited CachyOS files set both managers to 10 s but leave `user@.service`'s upstream timeout (120 s in a default build) untouched, so they keep the margin. Omarchy's `user@.service.d/10-faster-shutdown.conf` sets it to 5 s.

**Logout:** `omarchy-system-logout` runs `uwsm stop`. `wayland-wm@` propagates stop to `graphical-session.target`, and `app-graphical.slice` apps launched by `uwsm-app` have no own `TimeoutStopSec`, so a SIGTERM-ignoring app can hold logout for up to 90 s today and 5 s with this PR. Source analysis only.

**Verified:**
- The user manager reads `/etc/systemd/user.conf.d/*.conf`, `[Manager]` section only, and the compiled default is 90 s.
- New installs and the quattro upgrade get the file from `omarchy-settings` (`cp -a etc/.`).
- `test/shell.d/systemd-test.sh` passes 14 assertions at head; the new user drop-in assertion fails against the base tree.
- `test/shell.d/upgrade-to-quattro-test.sh` passes at head.

**Related PR:** #9070 removes the final `--overwrite` list this PR adds to, and the two edits conflict there. Dropping the line, as suggested above, avoids that.

**Optional notes:**
- The new assertions do not check the `[Manager]` header: a copy with the key under `[Service]`, which systemd ignores, still passes. Matching `^\[Manager\]$` as well would catch it.
- `omarchy-settings` lists the sibling faster-shutdown drop-ins in `backup=()` but not this one, so an administrator's edit would be replaced on upgrade. A matching change in omarchy-pkgs would keep it consistent.
- A `DefaultTimeoutStopSec` set in `~/.config/systemd/user.conf` no longer applies, because drop-ins take precedence over main files; a drop-in in `~/.config/systemd/user.conf.d/` named to sort after `10-faster-shutdown.conf` can still override it.
</details>
